title: Scheduled Jobs
readerIntent: Understand governed timed and manual execution.
priorKnowledge: Understand modules, services, and service identity.
summary: Persisted tenant job definitions schedule approved handlers on eligible module nodes; in-memory schedules are disposable and never the authority.

sections.heading: What is Scheduled Jobs?
paragraphs: A scheduled job is work that starts at a configured time or interval instead of from an immediate user request. Typical examples include reconciliation, cleanup, report generation, import, and maintenance.

It resembles a recurring calendar task assigned to an accountable service. The schedule starts the work, but identity, permission, retry, concurrency, history, and recovery still require explicit governance.

sections.heading: Business uses
items: Scheduled synchronization, reconciliation, cleanup, reminders, reporting, and integration work.
Authorized manual runs using the same definition and handler contract.
Node placement and temporary failover without turning servers into capability owners.

sections.heading: Boundaries
items: CronJob triggers work; services own business behavior and workflows own durable multi-step processes.
Manual execution cannot bypass tenant, node eligibility, permissions, overlap protection, or diagnostics.
Remote calls use service identity and target authorization, never human credentials.

sections.heading: Definition and runtime schedule
paragraphs: The persisted job definition is authoritative. A runtime scheduler creates disposable in-memory schedules for definitions assigned to an eligible node. Restart rebuilds them idempotently.
Editing or losing an in-memory timer never changes the persisted business schedule.

sections.heading: Example: stock reconciliation
paragraphs: Inventory owns a reconciliation service comparing stock balances and movements. CronJob owns when the approved handler runs and which eligible node acquires it.
A manual run invokes the same definition with authorization and audit; it does not call an arbitrary service name supplied by the browser.

sections.heading: Scheduling decisions
items: Time zone, expression, start, end, and missed-run policy.
Node eligibility, concurrency, overlap, and distributed acquisition.
Timeout, retry, idempotency, reconciliation, and compensation.
Input references, secrets, retention, permissions, and diagnostics.

sections.heading: When not to use a job
items: Use a normal service for immediate synchronous work.
Use an event consumer for reaction to a completed fact.
Use a workflow for durable manual and automatic business actions.
Use a data processor for high-volume partitioned processing.
Do not poll unnecessarily when an owned event contract exists.

sections.heading: What operators and business owners can expect
paragraphs: A scheduled job is visible as an owned, tenant-aware definition rather than an invisible operating-system timer. Teams can explain what it does, when it may run, which node is eligible, what happened on the last execution, and how a failure is recovered.

High-volume or financially sensitive work still requires capacity planning, idempotency, reconciliation, bounded retries, audit retention, and an explicit missed-run decision. Scheduling alone does not make a business operation safe.
